questions.q: Name the geometric figure represented by each: (i) The edge of a ruler from the 2 cm mark to the 8 cm mark. (ii) Sunlight coming through a small hole in a curtain. (iii) Three dots marked on a curved wire.
questions.a: (i) Line segment — it has two fixed endpoints (2 cm and 8 cm marks). (ii) Ray — it starts at the hole (initial point) and travels infinitely in one direction. (iii) Non-collinear points — they lie on a curved wire, so no single straight line passes through all three. A wrong answer like calling (ii) a line segment reveals the student thinks a ray has a second endpoint; calling (iii) collinear reveals they confuse "lying on a curve" with "lying on a straight line".

questions.q: Explain why $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BA}$ are different rays, but $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BA}$ represent the same line segment.
questions.a: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ has initial point A and extends infinitely through B; $\overrightarrow{BA}$ has initial point B and extends infinitely through A — they point in opposite directions (opposite rays). $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BA}$ both consist of exactly the same set of points between A and B, so they are identical; length and midpoint are unchanged. A wrong answer claiming they are the same ray shows the student ignores the initial point; claiming the segments are different shows they think order of endpoints changes the segment.

questions.q: Points A, B, C lie on a line such that B is between A and C. If AB = 3.5 cm and BC = 4.2 cm, find AC. Then state whether A, B, C are collinear and justify.
questions.a: Since B lies between A and C on the same line, AC = AB + BC = 3.5 + 4.2 = 7.7 cm. Yes, A, B, C are collinear because they all lie on the same straight line (given B is between A and C on that line). A wrong answer like AC = |3.5 − 4.2| = 0.7 cm reveals the student incorrectly applies the "difference of segments" rule meant for when a point lies outside the segment; not justifying collinearity reveals they treat it as a definition rather than a condition to verify.

questions.q: In the figure, line l passes through points P and Q. Point R is marked not on line l. A student says: "P, Q, R are collinear because I can draw a line through P and R, and another through Q and R." Identify the flaw in this reasoning.
questions.a: Collinear means a **single** straight line passes through **all three** points simultaneously. The student draws two different lines (PR and QR), which only proves each pair is collinear pairwise — not that all three lie on one line. Since R is not on line l (which contains P and Q), no single line contains P, Q, and R. A wrong answer accepting the student's reasoning reveals the confusion between "pairwise collinear" (always true for any two points) and "collinear as a set of three" (requires one common line).

questions.q: A classmate draws $\overrightarrow{XY}$ and labels the initial point as Y and the arrow pointing towards X. Is this correct? If not, correct the notation and explain the error.
questions.a: Incorrect. The notation $\overrightarrow{XY}$ means initial point is X and the ray extends through Y. If the initial point is Y and it extends through X, the correct notation is $\overrightarrow{YX}$. The error is reversing the order of letters — the first letter must always be the initial point. A wrong answer saying "it's fine, order doesn't matter" reveals the student treats ray notation like segment notation, ignoring directionality.

questions.q: Create a real-life scenario (different from the walkthrough) involving a ray, a line segment, and three collinear points. Draw a rough sketch and label all parts with proper geometric notation.
questions.a: Example: A straight railway track — the track from station A to station B is $\overline{AB}$ (line segment); the beam of the train's headlight starting at the engine (point E) and going forward is $\overrightarrow{EF}$ (ray); three signal poles P, Q, R standing exactly along the straight track are collinear points. A good answer includes a labelled sketch, correct notation ($\overline{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{EF}$, P, Q, R on one line), and distinct contexts for each. A poor answer uses the same object for all three or draws non-collinear points for the collinear example, showing they cannot distinguish the concepts in a novel setting.
